The Oxford Olympics Study 2016 estimated the out-turn cost of the Rio 2016 Summer Olympics at US$4.6 billion in 2015-dollars. This figure included sports-related costs, that is, (i) *operational costs* incurred by the organizing committee to stage the Games, of which the largest components were technology, transportation, workforce, and administration costs, while other operational costs included security, catering, ceremonies, and medical services, and (ii) *direct capital costs* incurred by the host city and country or private investors to build the competition venues, the Olympic village, international broadcast center, and media and press center, which were required to host the Games.[[66]](#cite_note-cost-69)

Indirect capital costs were not included, such as for road, rail, or airport infrastructure, for hotel upgrades, or other business investment incurred in preparation for the Games but not directly related to staging the Games. The Rio Olympics' cost of US$4.6 billion compares with costs of US$40–44 billion for [Beijing 2008](/wiki/Beijing_2008 "Beijing 2008") and US$51 billion for [Sochi 2014](/wiki/Sochi_2014 "Sochi 2014"), the two most expensive Olympics in history. The average cost of the Summer Games since 1960 is US$5.2 billion.[[66]](#cite_note-cost-69)

Sable bitch (left) and dog (right)

The breed was named *Deutscher Schäferhund*, by von Stephanitz, translating to "German Shepherd Dog."[[21]](#cite_note-fci-22) At the time, all other herding dogs in Germany were referred to by this name; they thus became known as *Altdeutsche Schäferhunde*, or [old German herding dogs](/wiki/Old_German_herding_dogs "Old German herding dogs").

The direct translation of the name was adopted for use in the [stud-book](/wiki/Stud-book "Stud-book"); however, at the end of the [First World War](/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), it was thought that use of the word "German" would harm the breed's popularity[[22]](#cite_note-palika-22-23) [in countries that had fought Germany](/wiki/Anti-German_sentiment#First_World_War "Anti-German sentiment").[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERice199912-24) The breed was officially renamed by the UK Kennel Club to "Alsatian Wolf Dog,"[[22]](#cite_note-palika-22-23) after the French region of [Alsace](/wiki/Alsace "Alsace") bordering Germany.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKern199011–21-6)

Eventually, the appendage "wolf dog" was dropped,[[22]](#cite_note-palika-22-23) after numerous campaigns by breeders who were worried that becoming known as a [wolf-dog hybrid](/wiki/Wolf-dog_hybrid "Wolf-dog hybrid") would affect the breed's popularity and legality.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKern199011–21-6) The name Alsatian remained for five decades,[[22]](#cite_note-palika-22-23) until 1977, when successful campaigns by dog enthusiasts pressured the British kennel clubs to allow the breed to be registered again as German Shepherds.[[24]](#cite_note-germanculture-25) The word "Alsatian" once appeared in parentheses as part of the formal breed name of the American Kennel Club, until removed in 2010.[[25]](#cite_note-26)

During the first decades of the 20th century, Penn made strides and took an active interest in attracting diverse students from around the globe. Two examples of such action occurred in 1910. Penn's first director of publicity, created a recruiting brochure, translated into Spanish, with approximately 10,000 copies circulated throughout Latin America. That same year, the Penn-affiliated organization, the Cosmopolitan Club, started an annual tradition of hosting an opening "smoker," which attracted students from 40 nations who were formally welcomed to the university by then-vice provost [Edgar Fahs Smith](/wiki/Edgar_Fahs_Smith "Edgar Fahs Smith") (who the following year would start a ten-year tenure as provost)[[80]](#cite_note-PennHistory-90)[[81]](#cite_note-NIE-91)[[82]](#cite_note-Klickstein-92)[[83]](#cite_note-CHM-93)[[84]](#cite_note-Collier-94) who spoke about how Penn wanted to "bring together students of different countries and break down misunderstandings existing between them."[[55]](#cite_note-Arch-Timeline-1740-64)

**Bruiser and Marigold** are the costumed bear [mascots](/wiki/Mascot "Mascot") of Baylor University.

Even though Baylor began its intercollegiate athletics in the 1890s, they did not have an official mascot until 1914. President [Samuel Palmer Brooks](/wiki/Samuel_Palmer_Brooks "Samuel Palmer Brooks") held a vote to choose a mascot from dozens of options including the buffalo, bookworm, antelope, and ferret. It was then when the student body decided to pick an [American black bear](/wiki/American_black_bear "American black bear") as their new mascot. In 1917, troops of the 107th Engineers donated a live bear named Ted to the university. Ted made his debut at the 1917 Baylor–[Texas A&M](/wiki/Texas_A%26M_University "Texas A&M University") football game.[[73]](#cite_note-73) Many years later, a costumed bear first made its appearance at the start of Baylor's 1981–1982 basketball season. This version of the bear did not last too long as a different version of the bear appeared in mid- to late-1980s.

Bruiser was modified two more times until the current version of Bruiser was introduced in late 2000s. In 2017, Baylor Spirit introduced Marigold as Bruiser's partner.[[74]](#cite_note-74) Marigold is usually seen wearing a yellow [Baylor Line](/wiki/Baylor_Line "Baylor Line") jersey.

Cartland left behind a series of 160 unpublished novels, known as the *Barbara Cartland Pink Collection*. These were published in ebook format by her son, Ian McCorquodale; each month, a new novel was published from that collection until, in 2018, all 160 novels had been published.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)

In 2010, to mark the 10th anniversary of her death, Cartland's first novel, *Jig-Saw* (first published in 1925), was reprinted.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

"As a tribute to Her Majesty the Queen on her [Diamond Jubilee](/wiki/Diamond_Jubilee "Diamond Jubilee") and to Barbara's enduring appeal to romantics everywhere, her publishers have re-released her catalogue collection, entitled – "The Eternal Collection". This collection, released beginning in November 2013, includes some novels published at the time [Queen Elizabeth II](/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") ascended to the throne in 1952.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)

In addition, her collections of [ebooks](/wiki/Ebooks "Ebooks") are available in Spanish, Italian, German and Dutch.

This is a list of the tallest players in [National Basketball Association](/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") history. It is currently topped by the 7-foot-7-inch (2.31 m) [Romanian](/wiki/Romanians "Romanians") [Gheorghe Mureșan](/wiki/Gheorghe_Mure%C8%99an "Gheorghe Mureșan"), taken by the [Washington Bullets](/wiki/Washington_Bullets "Washington Bullets") as the number 30 overall pick in the [1993 NBA draft](/wiki/1993_NBA_draft "1993 NBA draft").[[1]](#cite_note-draft-1)

As of the [2025–26 NBA season](/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_NBA_season "2025–26 NBA season"), thirty players have been listed at 7-foot-3-inch (2.21 m) or taller. Three are active as of the [2025–26](/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_NBA_season "2025–26 NBA season") season: [Victor Wembanyama](/wiki/Victor_Wembanyama "Victor Wembanyama") of the [San Antonio Spurs](/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs"), [Zach Edey](/wiki/Zach_Edey "Zach Edey") of the [Memphis Grizzlies](/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies "Memphis Grizzlies"), and [Rocco Zikarsky](/wiki/Rocco_Zikarsky "Rocco Zikarsky") of the [Minnesota Timberwolves](/wiki/Minnesota_Timberwolves "Minnesota Timberwolves"). The tallest player inducted into the [Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame](/wiki/Naismith_Memorial_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame "Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame") is 7-foot-6-inch (2.29 m) [Yao Ming](/wiki/Yao_Ming "Yao Ming"). Yao, [Ralph Sampson](/wiki/Ralph_Sampson "Ralph Sampson") and [Arvydas Sabonis](/wiki/Arvydas_Sabonis "Arvydas Sabonis") are the only players 7-foot-3-inch (2.21 m) or taller elected to the Hall of Fame.

[Yasutaka Okayama](/wiki/Yasutaka_Okayama "Yasutaka Okayama"), a 7-foot-8-inch (2.34 m) Japanese basketball player picked 171st overall in the seventh round of the [1981 NBA draft](/wiki/1981_NBA_draft "1981 NBA draft") by the [Golden State Warriors](/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors"), is the tallest player ever to be drafted to the NBA.[[2]](#cite_note-2) However, he never played in the NBA.[[3]](#cite_note-oddities-3)
